BEGIN: "By default (without BEGIN), PostgreSQL executes transactions in "autocommit" mode, that is, each statement is executed in its own transaction and a commit is implicitly performed at the end of the statement (if execution was successful, otherwise a rollback is done)."
"BEGIN initiates a transaction block, that is, all statements after a BEGIN command will be executed in a single transaction until an explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK is given."

COMMIT: "All changes made by the transaction become visible to others and are guaranteed to be durable if a crash occurs." ROLLBACK discards all updates (round-1 evidence, sql-rollback.html); execution: after ROLLBACK count back to 12.

claim_verdicts.evidence: BEGIN: "Statements are executed more quickly in a transaction block, because transaction start/commit requires significant CPU and disk activity." Tutorial 3.4: without BEGIN "each individual statement has an implicit BEGIN and (if successful) COMMIT wrapped around it" -> one write alone or in a block pays one start/commit either way; claim now states exactly that.
Opinion mirrors outline item 3. Factual part: 13.3.2 "Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row."

issues.quote: While the block is open, the rows it changed are held: another transaction that wants to change the same rows waits for yours to end.
issues.text: The lesson uses 'transaction', 'transaction block', 'block', 'unit' and 'unit of work' for nearly the same thing. I worked out that a block is what BEGIN opens and that a single statement is also a transaction, but 'another transaction ... waits for yours' made me stop to check whether 'yours' is the block or something else.
issues.fix: In the `BEGIN` bullet of Core concepts, add one clause: 'the block is how one transaction spans several statements; below, "the unit" means the block's changes.'

issues.quote: A file that ended in `COMMIT` instead would leave both rows: its next run would print 13 for `orders_before` and then stop.
issues.text: The paragraph starts with why the two writes belong together (foreign key, quantity rule), then jumps to a what-if about COMMIT and a re-run; 'and then stop' comes before its reason. I re-read it to connect the two halves.
issues.fix: Start a new paragraph at 'A file that ended in `COMMIT` instead…', so the foreign-key reason and the re-run what-if are read separately.

issues.quote: The gain comes from paying the cost of starting and ending a transaction once for many writes instead of once per write, not from `BEGIN` itself
issues.text: The second misconception is one long paragraph carrying three ideas (speed is a side effect, where the gain comes from, rows held while open) plus the 'you notice this' scene. I read it twice.
issues.fix: Split before 'But every row the block has changed stays held…' so the speed point and the held-rows point are two short paragraphs.

issues.quote: 13, because the block ended by keeping both rows, and they are now part of the shop's own data
issues.text: q6 is answered by a near-verbatim sentence in section 5: 'its next run would print 13 for `orders_before`'. I can pick 13 by recall without reasoning about COMMIT.
issues.fix: Ask about a different observable of the COMMIT variant, e.g. what `orders_inside_transaction` or the second run's first error would be, so the answer is not a copied line.

issues.quote: Fewer writes to disk is a real gain from one block, so the night's many small `INSERT`s can themselves finish sooner
issues.text: q4 option b: 'can themselves finish sooner' is awkward; I paused on whether 'themselves' means the INSERTs alone vs. the whole job. Still decidable from section 6, but b and d sit close.
issues.fix: Drop 'themselves': '…so the night's many small `INSERT`s can finish sooner.'
